h1: Remove an image background, in your browser
lede: Drop in a picture and the background comes off. Nothing is uploaded, nothing is queued, and there is no watermark — the whole thing runs on your own device.
a11y.canvas: Image preview with the background removed
common.notSaved: Your browser is blocking local storage, so settings will reset when you close the tab.
drop.title: Drop an image here
drop.hint: Or paste one, or choose a file.
drop.privacy: Your image stays on this device. It is never uploaded.
compare.hint: Switch between the original and the result. Shortcut: C
view.hint: Ctrl + scroll to zoom, drag to pan
mode.heading: How to find the background
example.heading: Not sure which to use? Try an example.
example.hint: Each loads a picture that mode handles well, with its settings already applied.
example.auto: A mug on a plain studio backdrop
example.color: A flat logo on white, with gaps inside it
example.chroma: A figure on an unevenly lit green screen
example.ai: A person in a cluttered room
ai.consentBody: This downloads a 7.6 MB model once. After that it is stored on this device and works offline, including with no connection.
ai.consentPrivacy: The model comes to your browser; your image still never leaves it. Nothing is uploaded either way.
ai.ready: Model ready, stored on this device. It will not download again.
ai.failed: The model could not be loaded. Check the connection and try again.
ai.note: AI mode finds the subject rather than matching colours, so it handles busy backgrounds. The edge is interpolated from a 320-pixel grid, so on a plain backdrop the colour modes still give a crisper one.
mode.hint.auto: Reads the colour around the edges and removes it. Best for a plain backdrop: product shots, scanned pages, studio photos.
mode.hint.color: You pick one colour and it goes. Best for flat artwork: logos, signatures, screenshots. Turn connectivity off to clear gaps inside letters.
mode.hint.chroma: Matches the hue, so a lit screen and its shadows go together. Best for green or blue screen footage and photos.
mode.hint.ai: Finds the subject instead of matching colours. Best for people and pets photographed in a real room, where colour matching cannot work.
adjust.heading: Adjust the cut
adjust.toleranceHint: How different a pixel can be and still count as background. Raise it if speckles are left behind, lower it if the subject is being eaten.
adjust.edgeShiftHint: Negative shrinks the subject to cut off a halo. Positive grows it back.
adjust.contiguous: Only the area connected to the edges
adjust.contiguousHint: Turn this off to clear background showing through gaps — the middle of an O, the space inside a handle.
adjust.decontaminateHint: Un-mixes the old background from semi-transparent edge pixels, which is what stops a white halo or a green rim.
brush.heading: Fix it by hand
brush.hint: Paint over anything the automatic pass got wrong. Strokes survive every other change, so you can keep adjusting afterwards.
out.heading: Output
warn.nothing-removed: Nothing was removed. Raise the tolerance, or switch to picking the background colour yourself.
warn.everything-removed: Almost everything was removed. Lower the tolerance — the subject is too close in colour to the background.
warn.busy-background: The background is not one flat colour, so an automatic cut will be rough. Picking a colour or using the brush will do better.
warn.mixed-background: One background colour has been removed, but part of the background is a different colour. Pick that colour with the eyedropper, or brush the rest away.
warn.empty: That image has no pixels to work with.
err.tooLarge: That file is over 50 MB. Try a smaller export of the same image.
err.badType: That file type cannot be opened. Use PNG, JPG, WebP, GIF, BMP, AVIF or ICO.
err.tooManyPixels: That image is too large to process in a browser tab. Scale it down and try again.
err.decode: That image could not be read. It may be damaged, or saved in a format this browser does not support.
err.unknown: Something went wrong reading that image.
err.exportFailed: The image could not be saved. Try PNG instead of WebP.
faq.a1: No. The page has no server to upload to. Your picture is decoded by the browser, processed by a worker running on your own machine, and discarded when you close the tab. You can check it yourself: open the network tab and remove a background — nothing is sent.
faq.q2: Is it really free, and where is the watermark?
faq.a2: Free, no account, no limit on how many images, and no watermark. The page is static files on free hosting, so once it has loaded there is nothing left to pay for and nothing to charge you for.
faq.q3: Will it cut hair out of a busy photograph?
faq.a3: No, and it says so rather than pretending. This works by matching colour, so it is excellent on a plain or near-plain backdrop — product shots, logos, signatures, screenshots, green screens — and poor on a subject photographed against a cluttered scene. Tools that manage that case run a neural network and need tens of megabytes of model weights downloaded first.
faq.q4: Why is there a faint outline around my cutout?
faq.a4: Edge pixels are a genuine mix of subject and background, so after keying they still carry the old background's colour. Leave "Remove colour fringe" on and it is un-mixed arithmetically. If a rim survives, nudge the edge shift negative by one or two to shave it off.
faq.q5: Why does part of my subject disappear?
faq.a5: Its colour is too close to the background. Lower the tolerance first; if that leaves speckles instead, keep the tolerance low and paint the rest out with the brush. On a photo with both a light background and a light subject, picking the exact background colour usually beats automatic.
faq.q6: Can I use the results commercially?
faq.a6: Yes. The image is yours, the result is yours, and there is no attribution requirement. Nothing is added to the file.
foot.privacy: Every pixel is processed in your browser. No account, no uploads, no watermark.
foot.disclaimer: Results depend on how distinct your subject is from its background. This matches colours; it does not recognise objects.

tool.meta.title: {tool} — Free, Private, No Upload
tool.edgeHeading: The part most tools get wrong
tool.auto.name: Background remover
tool.auto.description: Drop in an image and the background is detected from its edges and removed, with a transparent PNG out the other side.
tool.auto.intro: The default mode. It samples a ring of pixels around the border, works out which colour dominates, and removes everything connected to the edges that matches it.
tool.auto.point1: Detects the backdrop colour on its own — nothing to pick first.
tool.auto.point2: Tells you how uniform the border was, so you know whether to trust the result.
tool.auto.point3: Soft alpha at the boundary, so edges are not stair-stepped.
tool.auto.edge: Admitting when it cannot help. A colour-matching cut is excellent on a plain backdrop and poor on a cluttered one, and the difference is measurable before anything is removed — if the border is several unrelated colours, this says so instead of returning a ragged cutout and letting you work out why.
tool.auto.q1: What counts as a good background for this?
tool.auto.a1: Anything close to one flat colour: a paper backdrop, a studio sweep, a white product background, a screenshot, a scanned page. Gradients and shadows are fine as long as they stay in the same family — raise the tolerance to cover the range.
tool.auto.q2: What if the subject touches the edge of the frame?
tool.auto.a2: It still works, but the border sample will include subject pixels and the confidence reading will drop. Switching to colour mode and picking the backdrop directly avoids the problem.
tool.auto.q3: How large an image can it handle?
tool.auto.a3: Up to about 40 megapixels. The preview is computed at a reduced size so the controls stay instant, then the export is recomputed at full resolution.
tool.color.name: Colour background remover
tool.color.description: Pick one colour with the eyedropper and remove it everywhere, or only where it touches the edges.
tool.color.intro: Click the background with the eyedropper and that colour becomes the key. The useful part is the choice of whether to remove only the connected area or every pixel of that colour anywhere in the image.
tool.color.point1: Eyedropper picks the exact colour from your image, not an approximation.
tool.color.point2: Remove it everywhere, or only where it is connected to the border.
tool.color.point3: Recently picked colours are kept for reuse.
tool.color.point4: Tolerance is measured perceptually, so one setting behaves the same on light and dark colours.
tool.color.edge: Enclosed gaps. The hole in a letter O, the space inside a mug handle, the gaps in a lattice — all of them are background, and none of them touches the border. A connected fill can never reach them. Turning connectivity off clears them in one pass, which is the single most useful switch on a logo.
tool.color.q1: Why does my logo still have white inside the letters?
tool.color.a1: Because that white is not connected to the outside. Untick "Only the area connected to the edges" and it goes.
tool.color.q2: Does it match the colour exactly?
tool.color.a2: No, and it should not: compression and sensor noise mean a flat background is never one exact value. The tolerance sets how far from the picked colour still counts, measured in a perceptual colour space rather than in raw RGB.
tool.color.q3: Can I remove more than one colour?
tool.color.a3: One at a time, but the brush covers what is left over — and for a background made of two flat colours, running colour mode twice is usually quicker than fighting the tolerance.
tool.chroma.name: Green screen remover
tool.chroma.description: Key out a green or blue screen by hue, so lit and shadowed parts of the screen both go.
tool.chroma.intro: Chroma keying matches hue rather than overall colour. That matters because a lit screen runs from near-white at the top to nearly black in the shadows — enormously different as colours, almost identical in hue.
tool.chroma.point1: Keys on hue, so the whole screen goes even when it is unevenly lit.
tool.chroma.point2: Saturation and brightness floors protect dark hair and grey clothing.
tool.chroma.point3: Spill suppression pulls the green cast out of the subject.
tool.chroma.point4: Works on blue and any other screen colour, not only green.
tool.chroma.edge: Spill, and the floors that protect the subject. Light bouncing off a green screen tints the subject's shoulders and hair; removing the screen does not remove that cast. And a hue-only key with no brightness floor eats black hair, because a nearly black pixel has an unstable hue that can land anywhere. Both are handled here.
tool.chroma.q1: My subject has a green rim. How do I fix it?
tool.chroma.a1: Set "Neutralise colour cast" to green spill. It caps the green channel at the average of red and blue wherever green dominates, which removes the cast without touching anything legitimately green.
tool.chroma.q2: Does it have to be green?
tool.chroma.a2: No. Pick any screen colour with the eyedropper. Blue screens are standard where the subject wears green, and the keying works the same way.
tool.chroma.q3: Why is my dark hair disappearing?
tool.chroma.a3: That is the brightness floor being set too generously by a large tolerance. Lower the tolerance; near-black pixels then fall below the floor and are kept regardless of hue.
tool.replace.name: Background colour changer
tool.replace.description: Swap the background for a solid colour — white for a marketplace listing, a brand colour for a profile picture.
tool.replace.intro: Remove the background, then put a flat colour behind it instead of transparency. Marketplaces usually require pure white; profile pictures usually want something that is not.
tool.replace.point1: Preset swatches plus any colour you choose.
tool.replace.point2: Switching colour is instant — the cut is not recomputed.
tool.replace.point3: Blending happens in linear light, so edges do not darken.
tool.replace.point4: Output is fully opaque, which is what listing rules expect.
tool.replace.edge: Where the blend happens. Compositing a half-covered edge pixel using the values as stored makes it darker than it should be, which shows up as a dark outline on a light background. Converting to linear light first, blending, and converting back gives the colour that was actually there. It is the most common compositing mistake there is.
tool.replace.a1: Pure white, #ffffff, is what Amazon and most others specify. The first white swatch is exactly that, not an off-white.
tool.replace.q2: Can I put a photo behind instead of a colour?
tool.replace.a2: Not here. Export a transparent PNG and layer it over whatever you like in any editor — that keeps this tool to one job and does it properly.
tool.replace.q3: Why has my file got bigger?
tool.replace.a3: A flat background compresses extremely well in PNG, so usually it gets smaller. If it grew, the image is a photograph; switching to WebP will cut it substantially.
tool.brush.name: Background eraser brush
tool.brush.description: Paint away what the automatic pass missed, or paint back what it took by mistake.
tool.brush.intro: Automatic removal gets most of the way on most images. The brush covers the rest: erase a patch it left behind, restore a piece of the subject it ate.
tool.brush.point1: Erase and restore with the same brush — one checkbox switches direction.
tool.brush.point2: Adjustable size and hardness, so a soft edge stays soft.
tool.brush.point3: Undo stroke by stroke, with the usual keyboard shortcut.
tool.brush.point4: Strokes survive every other adjustment, so you can keep tuning afterwards.
tool.brush.edge: Strokes are stored where you drew them, not as pixels. The preview is a downscaled copy of your image, so a stroke recorded in preview pixels would land in the wrong place on a full-size export. Recording it in relative coordinates instead means the exported cut is exactly the one you were looking at.
tool.brush.q1: Do I lose my brushwork if I move a slider?
tool.brush.a1: No. Strokes are kept separately and reapplied after every recompute, so you can paint first and keep adjusting the tolerance afterwards.
tool.brush.a2: Yes — the undo button, or Ctrl+Z, removes the last stroke. "Clear strokes" removes all of them and leaves the automatic result.
tool.brush.q3: Can I use it on a touchscreen?
tool.brush.a3: Yes. The canvas handles touch and stylus input, and page scrolling is suppressed over it so a stroke does not drag the page instead.
tool.png.name: Transparent PNG maker
tool.png.description: Save a cutout as a transparent PNG or WebP, optionally trimmed tight to the subject.
tool.png.intro: The export side. PNG is the safe choice everywhere; WebP is the same transparency at roughly a third of the size, and every current browser reads it.
tool.png.point1: PNG for compatibility, WebP for size — both keep the alpha channel.
tool.png.point2: Trim to the subject, which removes the empty space around a cutout.
tool.png.point3: Exported at the original resolution, not at preview size.
tool.png.point4: The filename is derived from yours, so a batch of exports stays sorted.
tool.png.edge: Trimming keeps the feathered edge. Cropping to the last fully opaque pixel slices off the soft boundary that makes the cutout look natural — the bounding box here includes the partially transparent rim, so trimming never hardens an edge you deliberately softened.
tool.png.a1: PNG unless size matters. WebP is substantially smaller for photographs and is supported everywhere current, but a few older tools and some print workflows still refuse it.
tool.png.q2: Does saving as JPG keep the transparency?
tool.png.a2: It cannot — JPEG has no alpha channel at all. Anything transparent becomes black or white. That is why only PNG and WebP are offered here.
tool.png.a3: The original one. The preview is downscaled to keep the sliders responsive, but the export recomputes the cut at full size.
color.meta.title: Remove a {color} Background — Free Transparent PNG Maker
color.meta.description: Remove a {color} background from any image and download a transparent PNG. Start at tolerance {tolerance}. Runs in your browser — nothing is uploaded.
color.intro: Pick the {color} with the eyedropper and it is keyed out everywhere it appears. The numbers below are the ones this tool actually uses, so you can set it up in one go.
color.deltaE: Match radius at the suggested tolerance
color.when: A flat or near-flat {color} area that is clearly different from your subject. Compression noise and lighting variation are expected — that is what the tolerance absorbs. Where it struggles is a subject containing the same {color}, and there the brush is faster than any amount of slider tuning.
color.trait.neutral: Neutral colours sit near the centre of the colour space, close to every other greyish tone, so a generous tolerance quickly starts eating neutral parts of the subject. The suggested value is deliberately conservative — raise it only if speckles survive.
color.trait.near-neutral: This is only slightly off neutral, so it sits close to pale parts of most subjects. Keep the tolerance low and clean up with the brush rather than pushing the slider until the subject starts to go.
color.trait.saturated: A saturated colour sits far from skin tones, greys and most product colours, so there is plenty of room before the tolerance reaches anything you want to keep. That is why the suggested value is high.
color.trait.muted: A muted colour is close enough to browns and skin tones to need care, but far enough from neutral greys to take a moderate tolerance. The suggested value is a middle setting.
color.trait.dark: Dark colours compress poorly and carry most of an image's noise, so the tolerance has to cover a wider spread than the flat appearance suggests — while still staying clear of dark parts of the subject.
color.q1: What tolerance should I use for a {color} background?
color.a1: Start at {tolerance} and adjust from there. Raise it if flecks of {color} survive; lower it if the subject starts disappearing.
color.q2: It removed part of my subject as well. What now?
color.a2: The subject contains something close to that {color}. Lower the tolerance until the subject is safe, accept the leftover specks, and remove those with the brush — that is reliably faster than finding a tolerance that does both.
color.q3: Does it remove {color} inside the subject too?
color.a3: Only if you want it to. Leave connectivity on and only the area joined to the edges goes; turn it off and every matching pixel goes, including enclosed gaps.
format.meta.title: {format} to Transparent PNG — Free, No Upload
format.meta.description: Remove the background from a {format} file and download it as a transparent PNG. Runs entirely in your browser, with no upload and no watermark.
format.intro: Open a {format} file, cut out the background, and save the result as a PNG with a real alpha channel.
format.whyHeading: Why the output is a PNG
format.step1: Drop your {format} file onto the page, or paste it from the clipboard.
format.step2: The background is detected automatically; adjust the tolerance if anything is left behind.
format.step3: Use the eyedropper or the brush for anything the automatic pass missed.
format.step4: Choose PNG and download. The transparency is in the file, not faked with white.
format.alpha.binary: On or off per pixel only
format.alpha.yes.answer: Yes. {format} supports a full alpha channel, so transparency survives in the original format as well — but PNG is the safer thing to hand to someone else.
format.alpha.binary.answer: Only partly. {format} stores one fully transparent colour rather than a real alpha channel, so a soft edge cannot be represented and comes out jagged. PNG fixes that.
format.alpha.no.answer: No. {format} has no alpha channel at all, so transparency cannot be stored in it. Whatever you remove would come back as white or black. Saving as PNG is the only way to keep it.
format.alpha.yes.why: {format} can hold transparency itself, but PNG is understood by every tool, browser, document editor and marketplace without exception. Unless file size is the deciding factor, PNG is what to send on.
format.alpha.binary.why: {format} can mark one colour as transparent, and nothing in between. Every edge pixel is therefore either fully there or fully gone, which is what makes {format} cutouts look cut out. PNG stores partial coverage, so a soft edge stays soft.
format.alpha.no.why: {format} simply has no way to record that a pixel is transparent. This is the single reason "make my {format} background transparent" always ends in a different file type — there is nowhere in a {format} to put the information.
format.q1: Can a {format} file have a transparent background?
format.q2: Will the quality drop when I convert?
format.a2: Not from the conversion. PNG is lossless, so the pixels it keeps are exactly the ones it was given. Any compression artefacts already in the {format} stay as they are — converting cannot undo them, but it does not add more.
format.a3: No. The browser decodes it locally and the processing runs on your own machine. There is no server in this, which also means no queue and no file size limit beyond what your device can hold.

use.logo.intro: Logos are the easiest thing there is to cut out and the easiest to get subtly wrong. The colours are flat, so the match is clean — but the gaps inside letters are background too, and a connected fill will never reach them.
use.logo.why: Colour mode with connectivity off, so the counters inside O, A, P and R clear along with the outside. Tolerance stays low because a logo's colours are flat and exact; a high setting would start eating the lighter parts of the mark itself.
use.logo.watch: Check the inside of every enclosed letter and any gap in the mark before you export. A logo with one filled counter is the kind of mistake that survives all the way to print.
use.signature.intro: A signature photographed or scanned on paper is a near-perfect case: dark ink on a light, flat background, with nothing else in the frame.
use.signature.why: Colour mode on the paper with connectivity off, so the enclosed loops in letters clear too. The tolerance runs higher than for a logo because paper is never one value — it has texture, a scanner gradient, and usually a shadow.
use.signature.watch: Thin strokes and the faint tail of a pen lift are the first things to disappear if the tolerance goes too high. If the signature starts breaking up, lower it and brush out the remaining paper instead.
use.product-photo.intro: A product shot on a sweep or a sheet of paper is what this tool is best at. The backdrop is deliberately plain, which is exactly the condition colour matching needs.
use.product-photo.why: Automatic mode reads the backdrop from the border, and the default tolerance covers the shading a sweep naturally has. Connectivity stays on so reflections and highlights inside the product are kept.
use.product-photo.watch: Contact shadow. The shadow under a product is part of the backdrop to the algorithm and part of the photograph to you — decide which you want before exporting, and brush it back if the product looks like it is floating.
use.headshot.intro: A headshot against a studio backdrop cuts out well. One against a room does not, and no amount of slider tuning changes that.
use.headshot.why: Automatic mode with a slightly lower tolerance than usual, because skin tones and a light grey backdrop are closer together than they look. Decontamination stays on to stop a grey rim appearing around the hair.
use.headshot.watch: Hair is the limit of colour matching. Loose strands against a plain backdrop come out acceptably; a full head of fine hair against a textured wall will not. That case needs a neural network, not a colour match.
use.screenshot.intro: Screenshots are the cleanest possible input: the background is a single exact value with no noise, no compression artefacts and no lighting.
use.screenshot.why: Colour mode with a very low tolerance — the background really is one exact value, so there is nothing to absorb. Connectivity off, because UI screenshots are full of enclosed areas.
use.screenshot.watch: A screenshot saved as JPEG is no longer clean: compression spreads the background across dozens of near values and adds ringing around text. If the tolerance has to go above about 20, the file was re-encoded somewhere along the way.
use.sticker.intro: Stickers need a cutout with a soft, accurate edge, because the transparency is the whole point — they get pasted onto backgrounds you do not control.
use.sticker.why: Automatic mode with a generous tolerance and the feather left on, so the edge blends rather than showing a hard pixel staircase against whatever it lands on.
use.sticker.watch: Test the result on both a light and a dark background before using it. A halo invisible on white is obvious on black, and that is exactly where stickers end up.
use.stamp.intro: A stamp or seal photographed on a document has flat ink on paper, which keys cleanly — the complication is that the paper often shows through the stamp itself.
use.stamp.why: Colour mode on the paper with connectivity off, so the paper visible inside the stamp's design clears along with the surrounding sheet.
use.stamp.watch: Ink density varies across a rubber stamp. The faint parts are closest to the paper in colour and will go first, so check the lightest areas before settling on a tolerance.
use.qr-code.intro: A QR code is pure black on pure white with no intermediate values, which makes it the most forgiving input here — and the one where a mistake is most costly.
use.qr-code.why: Colour mode with a very low tolerance and connectivity off, so the white squares inside the pattern clear along with the surrounding margin.
use.qr-code.watch: Do not feather the edge and do not shift it. A QR code is read by thresholding, and a soft or shifted edge changes which module a scanner sees. Always scan the exported file before you use it anywhere that matters.
use.drawing.intro: A drawing photographed or scanned on paper behaves like a signature: dark lines, light background, nothing else in the frame.
use.drawing.why: Colour mode on the paper with connectivity off, so enclosed areas inside the drawing clear too. A moderate tolerance covers paper texture and the shadow a phone camera casts.
use.drawing.watch: Light pencil work and hatching are close in value to the paper, so they go first. If the drawing is thinning out, lower the tolerance and brush out the remaining background by hand.
use.sketch.intro: A pencil sketch is harder than an ink drawing: graphite is grey rather than black, so it sits much closer to the paper in colour.
use.sketch.why: Colour mode with a higher tolerance than ink needs, because paper photographed under room lighting varies a lot — but not so high that mid-grey pencil goes with it.
use.sketch.watch: The faintest construction lines will disappear before the paper is fully clear. If you need them, stop lowering the tolerance and finish with the brush instead.
use.scanned-document.intro: A scanned page is flat and evenly lit by design, which makes the paper trivial to key — the question is usually whether you want the paper gone at all.
use.scanned-document.why: Automatic mode handles the even scanner background without picking anything. The tolerance covers the slight gradient most flatbeds produce across a page.
use.scanned-document.watch: Transparent text is rarely what you want. For a document you intend to read, a white background is better; transparency is for overlaying a letterhead or a signature onto something else.
use.passport-photo.intro: Passport and visa photos are specified against a plain light background, which is precisely the case colour matching handles well.
use.passport-photo.why: Automatic mode with a conservative tolerance, because the required backgrounds are light grey or off-white and sit close to pale skin and light clothing.
use.passport-photo.watch: Check the official requirements before you submit anything. Most authorities specify an exact background colour, a head size and a margin, and a cutout alone does not make a photo compliant.
use.profile-picture.intro: A profile picture usually needs its background swapped rather than removed — a flat brand colour instead of whatever room it was taken in.
use.profile-picture.why: Automatic mode to lift the subject, then a solid colour behind it. Changing that colour does not recompute the cut, so you can try several in a second.
use.profile-picture.watch: Most platforms crop a profile picture to a circle. Leave room around the head, and check the result as a circle rather than as the square you exported.
use.ebay-listing.intro: eBay recommends a plain white background for listing photos, and photos that follow it demonstrably get more clicks than ones shot on a kitchen table.
use.ebay-listing.why: Automatic mode to remove whatever the item was shot on, then pure white behind it. Trimming tight to the item and letting eBay pad the frame usually looks better than an off-centre original.
use.ebay-listing.watch: A white item on a white background has no visible edge at all. Those need a coloured or dark backdrop when shooting — this cannot recover an edge the camera never captured.
use.amazon-product.intro: Amazon requires the main image of most products to be on pure white, and non-compliant images are suppressed rather than rejected loudly.
use.amazon-product.why: Automatic mode, then the pure white swatch — #ffffff exactly, which is what the policy specifies. The output is fully opaque, as required.
use.amazon-product.watch: The policy also covers how much of the frame the product must fill and bans added text, logos and borders. A white background satisfies one requirement, not all of them.
use.etsy-listing.intro: Etsy does not mandate white, but a consistent background across a shop is what makes a listing page look like a shop rather than a collection of snapshots.
use.etsy-listing.why: Automatic mode, then whichever background colour you have standardised on. Because changing the colour does not recompute the cut, doing a whole batch to one colour is quick.
use.etsy-listing.watch: Handmade items often have fuzzy or irregular edges — wool, paper, raw wood. Keep the feather on and avoid a negative edge shift, which would trim exactly the texture that sells the item.
use.thumbnail.intro: A cut-out subject on a bold flat colour is the standard thumbnail formula, and it works because the subject reads clearly at a very small size.
use.thumbnail.why: Automatic mode with a generous tolerance, since a thumbnail is seen small and a slightly rough edge is invisible at that scale. Then a saturated colour behind it.
use.thumbnail.watch: Check it at actual size, not zoomed in. Detail that matters at full size disappears entirely in a 120-pixel-wide thumbnail, and edge flaws you are agonising over will not be visible at all.
use.tshirt-design.intro: Artwork for printing has to have a genuinely transparent background — a white box around a design on a dark shirt is the classic and expensive mistake.
use.tshirt-design.why: Colour mode with connectivity off and a low tolerance, so every enclosed area clears and the artwork's own colours are untouched.
use.tshirt-design.watch: Soft edges do not print like they look on screen. Most printing processes threshold partial transparency, so a feathered edge becomes a ragged one. For print, reduce the feather to zero and accept a harder edge.
use.clipart.intro: Clipart is flat-coloured vector artwork saved as a bitmap, which makes it one of the cleanest things to key — the colours are exact and there is no noise.
use.clipart.why: Colour mode with a low tolerance and connectivity off. The background is one exact value, so there is nothing to absorb, and enclosed gaps are common in this kind of artwork.
use.clipart.watch: If the clipart was saved as a JPEG at some point, the flat colours are no longer flat and there will be a halo of intermediate values around every edge. Raise the tolerance a little and leave decontamination on.
use.icon.intro: Icons are small, flat and geometric, which means every pixel of the edge is visible and a sloppy cut shows immediately.
use.icon.why: Colour mode with a very low tolerance and no feather. Icons are usually exported from vector artwork, so the background is one exact value and the edges are already clean.
use.icon.watch: At icon sizes a feathered edge reads as blur, not as softness. Keep the feather at zero and the edge shift at zero, and let the original anti-aliasing do its job.
